subject: chemistry
unit_name: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
overview: This unit covers how organic compounds are purified, how their constituent elements (N, S, P, halogens) are detected, and how the percentage of each element is determined to arrive at empirical and molecular formulae. NEET regularly asks direct questions on Lassaigne's test colours, the choice of purification technique, Kjeldahl's limitations and short percentage-composition numericals. It is a high-scoring and largely fact-based unit.

topics.explanation: The choice of purification method depends on the nature of the compound and its impurities. Crystallisation uses the difference in solubility of the compound and its impurities in a suitable solvent; fractional crystallisation separates substances of similar solubility. Sublimation purifies solids that pass directly into vapour, such as camphor, naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid and iodine. Distillation methods depend on boiling points. Simple distillation suits liquids with very different boiling points. Fractional distillation suits close-boiling liquids, as in crude oil refining. Reduced-pressure distillation is used for liquids that decompose below their boiling points, such as glycerol from spent lye. Steam distillation suits steam-volatile, water-immiscible liquids such as aniline and essential oils. Differential extraction uses a separating funnel and an immiscible organic solvent. Chromatography separates components using a stationary phase and a mobile phase, through adsorption (column, TLC) or partition (paper).
key_points: Crystallisation: impure solid is dissolved in minimum hot solvent and cooled; activated charcoal removes coloured impurities
Sublimable solids: camphor, naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid, $I_2$
Simple distillation separates chloroform (b.p. 334 K) from aniline (b.p. 457 K)
Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column and is used for crude oil
Reduced-pressure distillation recovers glycerol from spent lye in the soap industry
Steam distillation: the liquid boils when $p_{water} + p_{organic} = p_{atm}$, so it distils below 373 K
Steam distillation separates o-nitrophenol (steam volatile because of intramolecular H-bonding) from p-nitrophenol
Differential extraction uses a separating funnel; continuous extraction is used when the compound is sparingly soluble in the organic solvent
Adsorption chromatography: column chromatography and TLC (silica gel or alumina as adsorbent)
Partition chromatography: paper chromatography, where water held in the paper is the stationary phase
Colourless spots are located by UV light, by an iodine chamber, or by spraying a reagent (ninhydrin for amino acids)
The less strongly adsorbed component moves faster and elutes first

formulas.formula: $R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance from base line}}{\text{distance moved by solvent from base line}}$
formulas.meaning: Retardation factor in TLC or paper chromatography; always less than 1
In steam distillation the mixture boils when the sum of the vapour pressures of water and the organic liquid equals atmospheric pressure

topics.neet_tip: Expect match-the-column or single-correct questions pairing a mixture with its purification method, plus questions on the meaning of $R_f$ and on steam distillation of aniline or o-nitrophenol.
topics.topic: Purification: crystallization, sublimation, distillation, differential extraction and chromatography

topics.explanation: Lassaigne's test is the standard method for detecting N, S, P and halogens. The compound is fused with sodium metal, which converts covalently bonded elements into ionic forms: $NaCN$, $Na_2S$, $NaX$ and $Na_3PO_4$. The fused mass is extracted with water to give the sodium fusion extract (SFE). Nitrogen gives Prussian blue with $FeSO_4$ followed by conc. $H_2SO_4$. Sulphur gives a black precipitate with lead acetate and a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside. When N and S are both present, insufficient sodium gives $NaSCN$, which produces a blood-red colour with $Fe^{3+}$. Halogens are detected with $AgNO_3$ after boiling the extract with $HNO_3$. Phosphorus is oxidised to phosphate and gives a yellow precipitate with ammonium molybdate.
key_points: Nitrogen: $6CN^- + Fe^{2+} \rightarrow [Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$
Prussian blue forms by $3[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-} + 4Fe^{3+} \rightarrow Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3 \cdot xH_2O$; the $Fe^{3+}$ comes from partial oxidation of $Fe^{2+}$
N and S together: $Na + C + N + S \rightarrow NaSCN$; then $Fe^{3+} + SCN^- \rightarrow [Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$, which is blood red
With excess sodium, $NaSCN + 2Na \rightarrow NaCN + Na_2S$, so the separate tests for N and S are seen instead of blood red
Sulphur with lead acetate in acetic acid: $S^{2-} + Pb^{2+} \rightarrow PbS$, a black precipitate
Sulphur with sodium nitroprusside: $S^{2-} + [Fe(CN)_5NO]^{2-} \rightarrow [Fe(CN)_5NOS]^{4-}$, a violet colour
Halogens: the extract is first boiled with $HNO_3$ to decompose $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, which would otherwise interfere
$AgCl$ is white and soluble in $NH_4OH$; $AgBr$ is pale yellow and sparingly soluble; $AgI$ is yellow and insoluble
Phosphorus: the compound is heated with $Na_2O_2$ to form phosphate, then boiled with $HNO_3$ and ammonium molybdate to give yellow $(NH_4)_3PO_4 \cdot 12MoO_3$
Hydrazine ($NH_2NH_2$) contains no carbon, so it cannot form $CN^-$ and gives a negative Lassaigne test for N
Diazonium salts lose $N_2$ on heating and also fail the test
topics.neet_tip: NEET asks for colours and formulae of complexes (Prussian blue, blood red, violet) and asks which biomolecules, such as the sulphur-containing amino acids, give positive N and S tests.
topics.topic: Qualitative analysis: detection of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens

topics.explanation: Carbon and hydrogen are estimated by Liebig's combustion method. The compound is burnt with $CuO$; the water formed is absorbed in anhydrous $CaCl_2$ and the $CO_2$ in $KOH$, and each is weighed. Nitrogen is estimated by Dumas' method, where it is converted to $N_2$ gas and its volume is measured. Alternatively, Kjeldahl's method converts nitrogen to $(NH_4)_2SO_4$; the $NH_3$ released with $NaOH$ is absorbed in a known excess of acid, and the remaining acid is back-titrated. Halogens are estimated by Carius' method: heating with fuming $HNO_3$ and $AgNO_3$ precipitates $AgX$. Sulphur is oxidised to $H_2SO_4$ and weighed as $BaSO_4$. Phosphorus is oxidised to $H_3PO_4$ and weighed either as ammonium phosphomolybdate or as $Mg_2P_2O_7$. Oxygen is found by difference.
key_points: Liebig method: $CaCl_2$ absorbs $H_2O$ and $KOH$ absorbs $CO_2$
Dumas method: hot $CuO$ converts N to $N_2$; the gas is collected over $KOH$ solution, and copper gauze reduces any oxides of nitrogen
Kjeldahl method is unsuitable for nitro and azo compounds and for nitrogen in a ring, such as pyridine
Kjeldahl method is widely used for foods and fertilisers
Carius tube contents: fuming $HNO_3$ plus $AgNO_3$ for halogens, or plus $BaCl_2$ for sulphur
Molar masses to remember: $BaSO_4$ = 233, $Mg_2P_2O_7$ = 222, $(NH_4)_3PO_4 \cdot 12MoO_3$ = 1877
Molar masses to remember: $AgCl$ = 143.5, $AgBr$ = 188, $AgI$ = 235
%O = 100 minus the sum of the percentages of all other elements

formulas.meaning: Hydrogen from the mass of water (Liebig)
Dumas method, with $V$ in mL at STP
Kjeldahl method, using the normality and volume (mL) of acid neutralised by $NH_3$

formulas.formula: $\%X = \frac{\text{at. mass of } X}{108 + \text{at. mass of } X} \times \frac{m_{AgX}}{m} \times 100$

topics.neet_tip: NEET checks the absorbents in Liebig's method, the compounds for which Kjeldahl's method fails, and direct substitution into the %N, %X and %S formulae.
topics.topic: Quantitative analysis (basic principles): C, H, N, halogens, S and P

topics.explanation: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. The molecular formula is the actual number of atoms in one molecule. To find the empirical formula, divide the percentage of each element by its atomic mass to get relative moles. Then divide each value by the smallest one. If the results are fractions such as 0.5 or 0.33, multiply all values by a suitable small integer to get whole numbers. The molecular formula is n times the empirical formula, where n = molar mass divided by empirical formula mass. The molar mass is often given directly or obtained from vapour density, since molar mass = 2 × vapour density.
key_points: Always find %O by difference before calculating moles
Do not round values like 1.5 or 1.33; multiply all values by 2 or 3 instead
n must be a whole number
Glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$), acetic acid ($C_2H_4O_2$) and formaldehyde ($CH_2O$) all have the same empirical formula, $CH_2O$
Benzene ($C_6H_6$) and acetylene ($C_2H_2$) share the empirical formula $CH$

formulas.meaning: First step in finding the empirical formula
Multiplier that converts the empirical formula to the molecular formula

topics.neet_tip: NEET usually gives percentage composition and vapour density or molar mass, and asks for the molecular formula.
topics.topic: Calculation of empirical and molecular formulae

topics.explanation: Numericals in this unit combine the estimation formulae with formula determination. In Dumas problems, correct the gas volume to STP. Subtract the aqueous tension from the observed pressure if the gas is moist, then apply the combined gas law. In Kjeldahl problems, find the acid actually neutralised by $NH_3$ by subtracting the acid neutralised by $NaOH$ in the back titration. Remember that $H_2SO_4$ is dibasic. In gravimetric problems, multiply the mass of precipitate by the mass fraction of the element in it. Worked example: 0.2475 g of a compound gives 0.4950 g of $CO_2$ and 0.2025 g of $H_2O$. Then %C = (12/44)(0.4950/0.2475)(100) = 54.5. Similarly, %H = (2/18)(0.2025/0.2475)(100) = 9.1.
key_points: Dumas: use $\frac{p_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{p_2V_2}{T_2}$ with $p_1 = p - \text{aqueous tension}$
STP values: 760 mm Hg and 273 K; 1 mol of $N_2$ (28 g) occupies 22400 mL
Kjeldahl: acid used by $NH_3$ = total acid minus acid neutralised by $NaOH$
Kjeldahl: $1\,M\,H_2SO_4 = 2\,N$
Fraction of the element in common precipitates: Cl in $AgCl$ = 35.5/143.5, Br in $AgBr$ = 80/188, S in $BaSO_4$ = 32/233
Check that all percentages, including oxygen, add up to 100

formulas.meaning: Converts a moist $N_2$ volume to STP; $f$ is the aqueous tension in mm Hg
Kjeldahl with $V$ mL of $M$ molar $H_2SO_4$, back-titrated with $V_1$ mL of $M$ molar $NaOH$

topics.neet_tip: Typical NEET numericals ask for %N by Kjeldahl or Dumas, or %Br or %S by Carius, in two or three steps using standard molar masses.

formula_sheet.meaning: Boiling condition in steam distillation, reached below 373 K
Blood-red colour, which shows N and S are both present
Violet colour from sodium nitroprusside, which confirms sulphur
Black precipitate with lead acetate, which confirms sulphur
Halogen identification after boiling the extract with $HNO_3$

common_traps: Assuming every nitrogen compound gives Prussian blue. Hydrazine has no carbon and diazonium salts lose $N_2$, so both give a negative test.
Expecting blood red whenever N and S are both present. The blood-red colour appears only when $NaSCN$ survives; excess sodium decomposes it into $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, which give the separate tests.
Adding $AgNO_3$ directly to the extract to test for halogens. $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$ must first be destroyed by boiling with $HNO_3$, or they will precipitate as $AgCN$ and $Ag_2S$.
Applying Kjeldahl's method to nitrobenzene, azo compounds or pyridine. Their nitrogen is not converted to $(NH_4)_2SO_4$, so the method fails for them.
Using the moist gas pressure directly in Dumas calculations. Subtract the aqueous tension first, then convert to STP.
Rounding 1.5 or 1.33 to the nearest integer in empirical formula work. Multiply all ratios by 2 or 3 instead.
Thinking that a higher $R_f$ means stronger adsorption. A larger $R_f$ means weaker adsorption, so the component moves farther.
Confusing distillation types. Glycerol needs reduced-pressure distillation, while aniline and o-nitrophenol need steam distillation.
quick_revision: Sublimation purifies camphor, naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid and iodine.
Steam distillation suits steam-volatile, water-immiscible liquids (aniline, essential oils, o-nitrophenol), which distil below 373 K.
Fractional distillation separates close-boiling liquids, as in crude oil refining.
Paper chromatography is partition chromatography; TLC and column chromatography are adsorption chromatography.
Lassaigne's test converts N, S and X into $NaCN$, $Na_2S$ and $NaX$.
N gives Prussian blue; N plus S gives blood red; S gives black $PbS$ or violet with nitroprusside.
$AgCl$ is white and dissolves in $NH_3$; $AgBr$ is pale yellow; $AgI$ is yellow and insoluble.
P gives a yellow ammonium phosphomolybdate precipitate.
Liebig method: $CaCl_2$ absorbs water and $KOH$ absorbs $CO_2$.
Kjeldahl: %N = 1.4NV/m; it fails for nitro, azo and ring nitrogen.
Carius method: $AgX$ for halogens, $BaSO_4$ (233) for S, $Mg_2P_2O_7$ (222) for P.
Molecular formula = n × empirical formula, with n = M/EF mass and M = 2 × VD.
